title: Derivatives as rates in context

draft.title: Derivatives as rates in context
card: The derivative dy/dx is the rate of change of y with respect to x. Its units are the units of y per unit of x.

If x(t) is displacement in metres at time t seconds, then x'(t) is velocity in metres per second. A positive value means moving in the positive direction, and a negative value means moving the other way.
To find a rate at a given time, differentiate first, then substitute the value of t. Example: V = 4t² + 10 litres at t minutes. V' = 8t, so at t = 3 the rate is 8 × 3 = 24 litres per minute.
The same idea works in any setting: if C(n) is cost in dollars for n items, then C'(n) is the rate of change of cost in dollars per item.
draft.remember: Differentiate, then substitute. The units are y units per x unit.

a.q: The volume of water in a tank is V = 5t² + 20 litres after t minutes. What is the rate of change of volume at t = 2?
a.why: V' = 10t, so at t = 2 the rate is 10 × 2 = 20 litres per minute. Substituting t = 2 into V gives 40 litres, which is the volume itself and not the rate.

b.q: A cyclist's displacement from home is x = 2t³ − 12t metres after t seconds. What is her velocity at t = 2?
b.why: x' = 6t² − 12, so at t = 2 the velocity is 6 × 4 − 12 = 12 metres per second. Substituting into x gives 16 − 24 = −8, which is her displacement in metres and not her velocity.
b.clue: Velocity is the derivative of displacement.
